posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
For me, the answer is to playtest quite a lot, and adjust things that seem to need it. It helps if you enjoy playing your own game.
My games tend to give the player choices over who is in the party. I try playtesting with different party compositions as well.

posts.author: DrFreeman
posts.body:
I use something like a check point system. Let's say there are 10 chapters to a story. By the end of the game with side quests, they're about level 50-60. Using a linear regression, that would be 5 levels per chapter. You could use a quadratic which is a bit more traditional to RPG Maker. The choice is yours. It gets XP out of the way.
Deciding the stats is dependent upon you and the player. The ideal state is to get players into a flow state like this diagram. There is a
good article
from Game Developer magazine on it.
Usually, it is best to have others play test the difficulty rather than yourself since game developers tend to have better skill. You have to balance tension and reward. Adding various dimensions to your combat is key. It can keep combat from getting stale. Similarly, effectively spacing out combat encounters so players look forward to unfolding your story. These are the typical combat design philosophies for JRPGs:
Players should be left with ~50% health after each encounter
Players should be left with ~80% health after each encounter
Players should be permitted to end with 100% health if they utilize highly advanced tactics
More modern games tend to favor being more soft on players with auto-saves, replay/rewind functions, or character swap after party members fall. The original Final Fantasy (on the NES) design was that every battle was to the death. It was unsurprising to not have about 50% health after many of the early battles. By the time you had the class improvement, many early battles were quite easy. In terms of my recommendation, I would say to strike a balance between what pleases your audience and what you would like to design.
Lastly with items, for many RPGs I hoard items, but never need them by the end of the game! Many players also prefer to play like that. The important aspect is that they have a bed where they can regularly recover at a reasonable cost. Otherwise, it can make grinding impossible. After that, measuring recovery items per encounter based on the ATB, defense, and attack. Maybe I take a sterile approach to game design?
There should be accountable and responsible designs that improve the players' quality of life. It involves consistently overcoming the next challenge until you can reach the ultimate rewards of the game. Pacing the rewards is often the percentage per encounter per chapter. Combat is relatively predictable, but difficult or combat is relatively unpredictable, but easy. A focus of strategy vs luck.
What kind of game themes are you emphasizing?
Strategy vs Grinding?
Stats vs Technology?
Abundance vs Survival?

My game is a little unique... There are no levels. The player get "EXP" from defeating enemies and they use that EXP to allocate to their main stats [HP, MP, ATK, ETC.], but it can also purchase certain skills as well [Sharpen, Mediate, ETC]. I also use a system that requires the player to equip their skills for battle. I feel this adds some strategy to the battle. Then there's the Augment System that adds to the stats and does other things like adds more skill slots [Or more Skill Tier Slots], etc... But I made it so that each piece of equipment has a certain number of slots that it can use for the Augments, but you need to have those slots "Punched" into the equipment before you can attach an Augment, which costs money. The Augment get progressively better stats as they go up in number, but I'm finding it hard to balance the cost of the Augments with the rise of the players in the game. Balancing the amount of money each item is and how much they could possibly have in the future of the game is difficult. I don't want the player to get a crazy good Augment and steamroll the game...
I've also made it a bit harder since I made the amount of Gold given by each enemy grow by a ratio of how much LUCK the party has. This is also how items and Gold are dished out from chests... More luck, more items and Gold.
I've made the "Everyday" items [Potions, etc.] incredibly cheap. I have no problem with them hording those. I have a problem with other things that could potentially break the balance of the game being easily accessible.
Oh, and the MC has to use various guns and bullets for his attack skills which you have craft [or pay the highway robber his money for them] which also costs money and forces the player to return to the main town periodically... Though this town is where the Room is and most of the side quests are given.
The enemy's stats rise with the players stats... I have this system working, but balancing it a bit tough. The information you have given me makes me feel like I get the balance working a lot better. I feel I have a little better understanding of how this balancing could work.
Thank you...

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Play testing is obviously very important. But I think another critical aspect is designing the game around what you perceive to be the most likely "average" player. There will always be min/maxers and people who do unconventional or unexpected (not average) things. But designing to the "average" will accommodate a large percentage of players.
For instance, if you have a generally static number of enemies in a particular area and the next area has an increase in enemy difficulty, then it would be important to test using an "average" party makeup to ensure that the player gets to the appropriate "level" or has the opportunity to earn enough points to allocate before heading to the next area.
Even if you have some random encounters, you could use the "average" amount of enemies that would reasonably be encountered by the "average" player and assign the EXP accordingly. Same with money and items. The more static your pool of treasure is, the easier it is to determine what most players would have access to at specific points. Notice I said "pool" of treasure and not specifically static treasure that every player is guaranteed to get.
I think you can design the framework and shell on paper, but play testing is where the truth of your design will be revealed.
In your example of not using levels and allowing the player to allocate points to stats free form, you would probably have to guess at how a reasonable, average player would make those allocations and go from there. You could use a + or - margin of error on allocation to ensure a decent range of what an average player might do.
Then, you could be relatively confident that you have accommodated an average player and that your game is not unbalanced in that perspective. The larger your "balanced" range of player potential behavior, the easier it is to justify that the game is balanced in spite of outliers who make unexpected decisions in allocation and end up having too difficult of a time.
One thing I would watch for is if there is a way to allocate points so the game is just too easy in any particular area. I would try to avoid the situation where if the player just dumps all allocation points into a couple of stats then they will cake walk the game.
Anyway, all of that is easier said then done and a lot of play testing is required. But again, I would focus on trying to determine an "average" player response and work from that.
Of course, this "average" determination is subjective and people play differently. Perhaps planning for an even distribution of allocation where the player is prioritizing stats for each particular character would be a good "average" starting point. This is especially true if you game provides hints to players about what stats should be prioritized for particular character types.
Not sure if any of that helps.
But one thing you could also do is think about a couple of games that you think are really well balanced and think about how they are designed. Think about all the different aspects and factors for that game and contemplate how you think the developers might have achieved that balance.
That is certainly something that I do. I look at my all-time favorite games and think about how I believe the developers achieved the balance that they did.
Good luck!

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
firestalker said:
So, Balancing the game is the hardest thing to do for me. Eventing a cutscene or mapping are nothing compared to trying to balance the enemies combat capabilities to the characters.
Click to expand...
The problem might be in what your damage formulas look like.  Or, in how you're approaching "balance".
Personally, I think the best approach to "balance" in terms of combat is "how many hits should the player character's die in?" and "How many hits should the enemies die in?"
Then, you playtest a lot to be sure that those remain the same across all combat (except for niche cases where you're fighting a Boss, or some ultimate challenge or something).
I have my game set up like this:
If you know nothing about the enemy, it's 4 actions to defeat it.
If you know the enemy's weakness, it's 1 action to defeat it.
If it's a boss, 20 rounds to defeat it if you refuse to learn and experiment, 10 rounds to defeat it if you know exactly what it's weak to.
Player characters go down in 5 hits, unless they have the wrong stuff equipped... then 1 hit.
All of this is "without buffs".  Buffs enemies use or players use will increase/decrease these times, but that's normal.  There's counter play to the enemy buffs where you can still defeat them in 1 hit, and enemies rarely have counter play to your own buffs, so you can extend survivability if you are one of those players willing to expend an action to do it.
firestalker said:
Nothing is harder than figuring out how much money items should be so the player can't get the best equipment 50% into the game. On that same note... Trying to figure out how much money the enemies should dish out in order to keep the player stocked but not overly.
Click to expand...
This one is a lot easier.
Let's say you have a Steel Sword available in the shop.  It costs 500 Gold to buy.  Okay, you want players to have to do, at minimum, 20 battles to afford it.  So, the enemy that is "the toughest" will give you the most Gold in the area... which means any combat encounter with it won't give anything more than 25 gold.
Pretty easy to figure that out.
What's harder to do is guess how much grinding a player is going to do for money.
Let me put it to you in a way that makes sense:
If you have a beginner shop in your game with a 10,000 Currency Sword, and enemies only drop 10 Currency a pop...
I'm grinding for it.  You made it available, so you are telling me I can have it.  So, I will get it, so I can probably break your game.  So I can be uber broken, REAL EARLY.
I might hate you for having to find 1000 battles to afford it, but I will do it ANYWAY and feel JUSTIFIED for doing it
Also, it should probably be noted:  I've never finished any RPG, to date, with less than 300,000 Currency in my pocket and nothing to spend it on.  More often, it usually ends up being 500,000 on average.
If you want me to spend currency, I need stuff to spend it on.  And consumables isn't a valid option unless every fight results in some damage that MUST be healed, or MP that MUST be restored.  Consumables are not a valid Gold Sink unless your combat relies heavily on using Consumables extensively.
So, if I've got nothing to spend my cash on, I'm going to hoard money.  And few RPG's find good ways for me to WANT to spend my cash.
firestalker said:
It's the hardest thing to do in my opinion...
SO! How do you go about balancing your game and making challenging, but not too challenging or easy?
Click to expand...
I find the hardest thing to do, to "signpost" what I expect of players.  There's universally players who never talk to NPC's, who skip important story bits, don't read flavor text...
Figuring out how to keep the "low IQ" players from borking themselves in a playthough is much harder in my opinion.  It's a lot like "design this as if the player were a toddler".
"If the player never talks to this person, how do I still get the information I need them to have, into their brains?".
As for challenge and gimmicks:
1.  Removed "Dedicated Healer" classes.  They make the game too easy.
2.  Required players to use consumables for all healing.
3.  Required players to learn what equipment protects them from, and use that to mitigate damage.
4.  Required players learn "enemy archetypes" so they can more easily guess weaknesses of enemies.
5.  The above mentioned "how many hits" stuff.
6.  Removing "direct power gain" from Level Ups.  You only get stats from completing quests.  But, gaining levels can give you access to new Quests.
7.  Enemies employ and rely upon gimmicks, rather than stats.  Stats are important, sure, but not as important as making the player cure a Poison that ticks down 20% of your health each turn.
8.  I use "low" stats and as a result "simplified formulas".  The basic damage formula is just a.atk - b.def.  Characters don't really start with any regular stat above 15.  Makes the formulas easier to balance, as well as predict "how powerful" a player will be with all the equipment and quests available to them at any given time.  I have a spreadsheet that lists what any potential stat spread will be by any point in the game.  I then utilize 60-75% of "max stat" as the balancing point.  If max Attack at this point of the game is 100, then the regular mooks will have about 60 Defense.  The boss will have 75% health.  Or whatever, within that rage.
Hope all of that helps.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Just as a heads' up:
If you have both Consumables and Healing Skills, you run the risk of two things:
1.  One of these being far better than the other, so the other is useless and never gets used (usually the MP healing version gets used, because on average, it's 6 times more efficient to heal via skill than consumable, even if it costs 3x as much to refill MP as it does HP).
2.  You risk "redundancy".  If both are equal in terms of effectiveness, you now have two systems that do the exact same thing, which isn't necessarily a good idea (at least, if you're like me and cut out systems that serve no purpose... like two systems that do the same thing).
---
I'm surprised you had enemies that could utilize the AI so effectively in the early game that they'd destroy you.
I ramp up through "mechanics".  The first enemies are "slimes" (as per usual trope, reason, thing, that a Quest Giver lampshades), and they merely demonstrate how "stats" work to the player.  The "next up" enemies could be Bandits, Wolves, or Poison critters.  Bandits and Wolves teach the player how "armor" works (physical damage is split into Slashing, Piercing, and Blunt types, each effective against specific kinds of armor).  Wolves, in particular, will merc you in one hit if you fail to equip either Cloth or Leather armor when you fight them (they use speedy attacks to hit you, which means they target your Reflex stat... and heavy Plate Armor drops your Reflex stat).  Like... they will hit you for around 40 damage if you have the wrong equipment on... but only about 3 damage if you're wearing what you SHOULD.  Wolves are also a "knowledge" check to a degree.  If you talk with an NPC, they will tell you that "Wolves run if you burn them real bad", which tells you that Wolves (and by Extension, anything that classifies as a "Beast") are weak to Fire).  And, if you do inflict "burn", they do escape combat.  Bandits teach you about Piercing attacks, mostly, and usually wear the Leather Armor you should have equipped for their dogs (which means you need to learn which weapon type is good against Leather Armor!).  The "Poison Critters" teach you weaknesses to plants, bugs, some beasts, and how to deal with Poison (it's a dungeon about Poison, and nearly everything in it will attempt to Poison you first turn).
The mechanics ramp up from there and slowly teach each thing the player will need to know.  Until, I'm teaching "tactics" to the players.  Tactics are more fun.  That's where I can troll the player
If you think up an overpowered tactic, my enemies will know it, or be immune to it sometimes, and also use it against you.  Or, they will combo stuff into you to wreck your team.
Mooks are the lessons.  Bosses are the test.

Just a heads up, be careful not to cause choice paralysis when players level up since it may be hard for them to make an reliably informed decision on what's best to use their EXP on.
With that being said, playtesting is really the only way. I know some want to get spreadsheets out and be all formulaic (what I used to do), and even if you do that and account for every digit, a game can sometimes be "too balanced" where everything feels the same in an attempt to make nothing stronger than anything which is why playtesting is best to see how the game feels.
